Attacks have recently been made in the Chinese communist press in Canton, Peking and Hong Kong against Canadian nuns of the Order of the Immaculate Conception who conduct the Orphanage of the Holy Child in Canton.
Typical charges made against the nuns are as follows:
1.	Far from pursuing acts of charity they are guilty of inhuman acts against the children in their charge.
2.	The orphanage is a typical example of an imperialist charity organization, operation of which would not be tolerated by the Chinese people.
3.	Since the communist liberation of Canton the orphanage had admitted a total of 2,251 infants, of whom 2,116, or 94 per cent, have died in the institution to date.

Inquiries of the Ministry
4.	This mortality rate reflects fully on the irresponsible attitude adopted by the sisters in caring for the infants.
This information, which we received from unofficial sources-that is the information as to these charges-has been confirmed by telegram from our high commissioner in London, who secured the confirmation from the United Kingdom authorities, who of course are represented in China.
A letter from the orphanage in Canton, dated March 5, has been received by the Mother Superior in Montreal. The nuns reported that the orphanage had been taken over by the Chinese authorities and that the Canadian nuns were to be deported to Hong Kong. There has been no official confirmation of newspaper reports of their arrest. The United Kingdom foreign office has been requested by the Canadian government to ask the United Kingdom charge d'affaires in Peking to do everything possible to assist these nuns who apparently have been the victims of grotesque and unfounded charges.

maintopic: QUESTION AS TO RECROSSING OF 38TH PARALLEL BY UNITED NATIONS TROOPS
QUESTION AS TO RECROSSING OF 38TH PARALLEL BY UNITED NATIONS TROOPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair I should like to take a few minutes to bring to the attention of the house a matter which I believe is of great concern, not only to the people of Canada but to the people of the whole western world. I refer to the fact that for the second time communist forces in Korea have been driven to or across the 38th parallel. I should like to know what action is to be taken by the United Nations forces when they reach the 38th parallel on this occasion.
On February 13 the leader of this group, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), asked a number of questions which were answered by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson). These will be found on page 306 of Hansard and are as follows:
Were members of the United Nations consulted about the reported recrossing of the 38th parallel by United Nations troops? If so, did Canada express an opinion, and what was it?
Has Canada made any representations to the Secretary General or to the United Nations concerning reconsideration of the implied permission which was granted to the troops last October?
The Secretary of State for External Affairs replied in part as follows-and I do not think I am leaving out any important part of his reply:
There is some doubt as to the exact details about the reported crossing of the 38th parallel by a South Korean detachment. Apparently it was a purely tactical movement and on a small scale, and does not indicate that any decision has been taken for a major crossing of the line, even if military conditions make that possible.
In reply to the second question, Mr. Speaker, Canada has not made any representations to the
Korea
Secretary General or to the United Nations concerning the question of the recrossing of the 38th parallel by United Nations forces. However, representatives of governments with forces participating in Korean operations have had informal discussions recently with the United States representatives in regard to this and other matters arising out of the Korean campaign. These discussions have included a Canadian representative. As a result of these discussions, I think I can state that the political significance of any new move across the parallel deep into North Korean territory is fully appreciated. At this moment I would not like to add anything to this observation beyond repeating my view that any decision taken in this matter should be a collective one, including particularly those governments who are participating in United Nations Korean operations, of which the most important is the United States of America.
I wish to draw attention to one sentence I have just read from the statement of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. It is as follows:
As a result of these discussions, I think I can state that the political significance of any new move across the parallel deep into North Korean territory is fully appreciated.
In other words, the military consequences of crossing the parallel last October are in the minds of the members of the United Nations, and particularly those who have representatives in the armed forces of the United Nations in Korea. So far as recrossing the parallel is concerned, the situation today is one that should not be left in doubt, and indeed in my opinion cannot be left in doubt very long, because if the United Nations organization itself does not take action in this matter, action may be taken by others. I maintain that the decision to recross the 38th parallel is a political decision and should be taken by the United Nations; the matter should not be left to any military general no matter how eminent he may be.
At this time the press is full of conjecture about what may happen. The question is discussed in newscasts. I believe that the government of this country, which has a military force with the United Nations forces, should not leave the country in the dark concerning what its attitude is witn respect to the recrossing of the 38th parallel. For my part I have always felt that it was a wrong policy to cross the parallel. I do not know whether any hon. members can recall the contribution I made to the debate last September, when we were discussing the sending of armed forces to Korea. I asked at that time what our attitude would be if we drove the North Koreans across the 38th parallel. I pointed out then that I did not believe we could unify North and South Korea under one government. I said in support of my argument that I had attended the United Nations assembly in 1947 when the commission on Korea was set up. I said that I had noted Soviet Russia's attitude at that

Korea
time to the commission, an attitude which has not changed since then, because the commission was never allowed to cross into North Korea. I said that if Soviet Russia had not recognized the United Nations commission in 1947 she was not likely to recognize it in 1950.
Perhaps I had better read to the house what I said at that time. As recorded at page 229 of Hansard for September 4, 1950, I said:
In my opinion we should without delay answer some of the questions people are asking. What are our intentions in Korea? If we succeed in driving the North Koreans back to the 38th parallel, are we going to stop there or are we going to go on beyond that? As this is a United Nations force, I agree that it is not altogether within our right to say what a United Nations army is going to do when it reaches that point; but our government certainly should make it clear what is their opinion on the issue.
I did not foresee that it would not be Russia but China that would come into the picture. However, whether it is Russia or whether it is China, I am satisfied that there is not the slightest hope of unifying Korea at this time under one government. In an article which I wrote on the Korean situation for a weekly paper in Vancouver in the first week of October I said that, in my opinion, for the United Nations forces to cross the parallel would needlessly and tremendously increase the danger of war. As it happens, it has been demonstrated that I was correct on that point.
I contended at that time, and I contend now, that so far as the United Nations forces are concerned this is not a war of conquest. It is not a war to destroy communism. It is not even a war, if there can be such a war, to prevent war. In Korea the United Nations took police action only, and in my opinion we are only justified in going as far as the boundary that was in existence and was recognized on June 25 last year.

maintopic: QUESTION AS TO RECROSSING OF 38TH PARALLEL BY UNITED NATIONS TROOPS
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question?

maintopic: QUESTION AS TO RECROSSING OF 38TH PARALLEL BY UNITED NATIONS TROOPS
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: QUESTION AS TO RECROSSING OF 38TH PARALLEL BY UNITED NATIONS TROOPS
speechtext: The hon. member says the boundary was recognized. The North Koreans, the Russians and the Chinese forgot to recognize it, and since then there has been practically no recognition of that boundary line. Nevertheless the hon. member must have reasons for saying that he thought it was a poor idea to pass that line. Will he give us the cold reasons why he came to that conclusion over and above the generals of the army?

maintopic: QUESTION AS TO RECROSSING OF 38TH PARALLEL BY UNITED NATIONS TROOPS
speechtext: I thought I had already given those reasons.

maintopic: QUESTION AS TO RECROSSING OF 38TH PARALLEL BY UNITED NATIONS TROOPS
speechtext: You gave your reasons, but why did you have those reasons?

maintopic: QUESTION AS TO RECROSSING OF 38TH PARALLEL BY UNITED NATIONS TROOPS
speechtext: I suppose I had those reasons because my mind worked that way.

maintopic: QUESTION AS TO RECROSSING OF 38TH PARALLEL BY UNITED NATIONS TROOPS
speechtext: Why?

maintopic: QUESTION AS TO RECROSSING OF 38TH PARALLEL BY UNITED NATIONS TROOPS
speechtext: I cannot say why my mind works in a certain way; I only know it does. I cannot tell why the hon. gentleman's mind works in a certain way; I just know it does. I doubt if anyone can tell why he thinks as he does.

maintopic: QUESTION AS TO RECROSSING OF 38TH PARALLEL BY UNITED NATIONS TROOPS
speechtext: But why did you come to the conclusion?

maintopic: QUESTION AS TO RECROSSING OF 38TH PARALLEL BY UNITED NATIONS TROOPS
QUESTION AS TO RECROSSING OF 38TH PARALLEL BY UNITED NATIONS TROOPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the previous speaker (Mr. Maclnnis) emphasized the extent of the devastation that is resulting from war being waged in Korea. There are three million people suffering privation and want such as the world has never known before. I am quite sure that the representatives of the various nations in the United Nations have made up their mind that they are going to stop wherever they possibly can, be it the 38th parallel or any other line, so long as that decision is in keeping with the situation as their generals in the field see it. The opinions of these representatives will be formulated at that time. I am quite confident that the generals in the field, who are tried and proven men, realize that the feeling of the people represented at the United Nations is that they do not want war.
There is one thing of which I am sure, and I believe and I hope that the majority feel this way: that when the troops fighting in Korea reached the 38th parallel and called upon the North Koreans, who were responsible for the suffering and devastation mentioned by my hon. friend, to stop fighting and when the North Koreans refused to do so, the generals handling the tactics of our armies in

Korea
Korea reported to the proper people in the United Nations that in their opinion we had better go after these fellows on the other side of the 38th parallel. We should dig them out, once and for all, and, if they could be apprehended, punish them for the atrocities they had committed. The North Koreans ignored the request of the United Nations for a cease-fire to discuss peace terms. They were impudent and arrogant, backed by Red Russia and the Red Chinese. When we ultimately arrived at the conclusion that it was necessary-and certainly the United Nations did not do so without a great deal of thought and concern about the ultimate results-our armies drove beyond the 38th parallel to the Manchurian border. They believed it was the right thing to do.
In my opinion all too frequently the question of the attitude of the Canadian government regarding our troops crossing the 38th parallel is raised in this house. The answer must be, and continue to be, that we will not cross it unless we have to do so. We will not cross it unless we think it is the best thing to do. If we have to cross it, we will. If we have to cross the Manchurian border, we will. If we have to go to Moscow, we will.

maintopic: QUESTION AS TO RECROSSING OF 38TH PARALLEL BY UNITED NATIONS TROOPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not altogether agree with the member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) that we should stop at the 38th parallel. I believe it depends to a very large extent upon the action or intention of the North Koreans and Chinese. If they are willing to have a ceasefire when we reach the 38th parallel, so that there can be a general discussion in the hope that we may reach some agreement, then of course we can easily stop at the 38th parallel. On the other hand, if the North Koreans and Chinese are not willing to have a cease-fire, then we have to remember that the 38th parallel is not a natural defence line. In that case I believe we should proceed to advance until we have reached a line that can be easily defended, and in Korea that might well be where the land narrows.
When the resolution to unify Korea was before the general assembly, I recall that it seemed to be the general understanding that we would advance a certain distance and then establish a neutral zone. It was certainly understood that we would not go right to the Manchurian border. I gathered that it was the understanding also that Syngman Rhee would not go beyond the 38th parallel but would remain in South Korea. I do not know whether he stayed in the south, but apparently he played an important part in making political appointments in North Korea. I believe we made a great mistake in advancing to the Manchurian border, and

also in allowing Syngman Rhee to make political appointments in North Korea.
During the special session last year I think I made it plain that I thought a mistake had been made in going into Korea at all. In the first instance I supported the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) when he refused to send troops there. Many members stated we had gone into Korea to liberate the South Koreans. At that time I ridiculed the idea, and pointed out that we were going there for one purpose only, and that was to establish the prestige of the United Nations organization so that it might be a warning to the communist armies that if they committed an act of aggression at any time they would be met by the armed forces of the United Nations. How can anyone talk about liberating people when you have to go there and smash the country and bring about the wholesale slaughter of the people? At that time I ridiculed the idea that you could have such a thing as collective security. There is no such thing. Collective action, yes, but collective action and collective security are two totally different things. We shall never have security until the member nations of the United Nations organization are willing to live up to the principles of the charter. Until that is accomplished, there will never be collective security.
We hear a lot of criticism of General MacArthur. No doubt he has made many unwise statements. On the other hand, he is in a position in which I do not believe any other general has ever been. He is in the position of having to fight an enemy with one arm tied behind his back. He is having to fight an army that is allowed to attack him from any point, while he is not allowed to attack the supply bases of the army attacking him. That is not fair to the fighting men of Canada, the fighting men of the United States, or the fighting men of our allies. Unless we can place our armies in such a position that they will be free to counterattack the enemy at any point from which the enemy may come, then I believe we would be well advised to pull out of Korea entirely. We should draw a line, we will say through Formosa, and say: Now, if you cross that line it means war. In order to cross that line the enemy would have to have a navy. It would be an easy thing for us to stop the enemy at that point. I cannot see why we should allow the communist forces to choose the field of battle in every instance. I repeat that it is time that we chose the battleground and said: If you cross this line or that line, it means war. But let us choose a line that will be to our advantage instead of letting the enemy choose a line that is always to their advantage.

maintopic: QUESTION AS TO RECROSSING OF 38TH PARALLEL BY UNITED NATIONS TROOPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I disagree somewhat with the position taken by my colleague the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis). I think it would be a mistake for the United Nations to state definitely that it was their policy to stop at the 38th parallel. It would be just as great a mistake or even greater to advance so far in North Korea that again we seem to the Chinese to threaten their territory. Nevertheless this debate points up one of the most important aspects of the whole situation, and that is the essential need for civilian control over the commanders in the field. I am not certain that that objective has yet been achieved; but at the moment, so far as the tactics of the day are concerned, I believe the commanders in the field must have a reasonably free hand to decide how far they will go to secure a position which will be militarily defensible. After all, they must think of the lives of the men who are operating under them.
The commanders in the field must also consider this fact: They cannot attack the source of supply without declaring war on China; and I do not think any of us want that. Therefore all they can do is to attack the supply lines of these alleged Chinese volunteers-who are, of course, members of the Chinese army; and that can only be done in a satisfactory way if the supply line is fairly long. I reiterate my opinion that it would be a mistake just now to say definitely that it is our intention to stop at the 38th parallel.

maintopic: QUESTION AS TO RECROSSING OF 38TH PARALLEL BY UNITED NATIONS TROOPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of offering any opinion on the strategic or tactical situation.
I want to make just one or two brief remarks.
I well remember my feeling on October 12 last, which I think was the date on which the 38th parallel was crossed previously. It was simple. I did not have any wisdom before the event. I did not have any extremely strong views. I just had this feeling: "I hope they know what they are doing." In retrospect, it seems to me that it is not clear that they did know what they were doing then. They disregarded the strong suggestion that had come from India as to what would be the effect of crossing the parallel. As a matter of fact, though it is a view that I personally abominate, I know that there is a strong view held by many in England-what we will call the leftist view in England-that we were grievously at fault.

maintopic: QUESTION AS TO RECROSSING OF 38TH PARALLEL BY UNITED NATIONS TROOPS
speechtext: And by some Conservatives.

maintopic: QUESTION AS TO RECROSSING OF 38TH PARALLEL BY UNITED NATIONS TROOPS
speechtext:
That may be so. We will say it is a view that is quite broadly held in England. I happen to have seen it in an article written by G. D. H. Cole.
80709-92J
Korea
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) may be quite right in saying that others had that view. I was astounded by that article and the want of sympathy it indicated with the course that had been taken. That is, however, merely a digression. What I want to come back to is to make this point quite simply.
It seems to me that we now have what one so seldom gets, namely a second chance-a chance to consider this situation. We have, as I see it, this unusual situation. Elements, at any rate, in the high command-men like Eisenhower and those who take what we may call the European view-certainly desire any chance with honour, or even with face-saving, which would enable us to disengage in Korea so as to be stronger elsewhere. My point is this. I believe that the ordinary man in the street in Canada also has that feeling strongly, I therefore merely wish to reiterate what the hon. member for Vancouver East has said, and say that I hope at this time it will be possible for the minister to take us more into his confidence than he has felt able to do up until now.
I do not wish to dissociate myself from what has been said about the military difficulties. Any man who knows the least thing about military operations knows that you cannot give a man a job to do and then prevent him from doing it. We all realize the difficulties in which they have been situated. I do not wish to see the commanders in the field with their hands tied so that they cannot carry out what they should do. I am only suggesting-and I understand it was the suggestion made by the hon. member for Vancouver East-that at this time, when we have a second chance, the matter should be again, reviewed, as I am sure it is being reviewed in all its aspects, and that the people of Canada should know as much as they can know about the situation now; because I believe that in overwhelming majority what they would like is that in some way this thing be stopped here and now.

maintopic: QUESTION AS TO RECROSSING OF 38TH PARALLEL BY UNITED NATIONS TROOPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think we should lose sight of the point of the speech made by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis). The speech which has just been made by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) and the one made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart) show clearly, I think, that these views about the situation in Korea cut right across party lines and thinking. When I suggested to the hon. member for Greenwood that there were Conservatives in Britain who took the same view as Mr. G. D. H. Cole, I had in mind particularly one or two leading articles I read

Korea
in the London Times. The London Times is by no stretch of the imagination a leftist paper, but it has been critical of the operations in Korea. I think what my hon. friend, was really trying to impress on the minister and the house was that decisions that must be made to carry on this war must be political decisions; that is to say, they must be made by the political representatives of the countries that are associated in the United Nations, and particularly by the countries that are associated in the Korean affair. The fear that many people have is that this will not be done.
I was not at the United Nations assembly, as it happened, for some few days before the actual resolution was passed to cross the 38th parallel but I can remember distinctly last autumn the hesitation on the part of those of us who were there to accept the proposal when it was first made. I also remember that subsequently, in the month of November, we thought that a halt would be called and that negotiations would be opened long before the armies approached the Yalu river. But the political decision, if there was a political decision-or perhaps I should say this political understanding- was overriden by the general in the field. He may have been in consultation with his headquarters at Washington; even of that we were not particularly sure, but in any event he seemed to be paying little attention to what was, I believe, the opinion of a large group of nations in the United Nations.
Then there is what the hon. member for Greenwood has said about the constant warning that was given by India, an Asiatic nation knowing something of the feeling of these millions of people on the continent of Asia. I have no doubt that the minister of external affairs has expressed a view on this matter. But the important thing is this. I agree with the hon. member for Greenwood that not only the people of Canada but, if public opinion polls are to be relied upon, the people of the United States as well as the people of the United Kingdom, are anxious that there shall be a speedy end to this Korean campaign, with the greatest possible degree of honour to the United Nations. I believe they realize, as most of us do, that the real struggle and the real danger at the moment is not in Asia, but in western Europe, and that if we are persuaded to divert our attention and our energies to the Far East we are endangering the situation in the more vital centre elsewhere.
I agree with what was said by the hon. member for Vancouver East and the hon. member for Winnipeg North, that in order to meet the threat of communism we should
[Mr. Coldwell.l
be paying much more attention to economic aid for these people than we have been.
What I really rose to say was that I hope we shall not miss the point of the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver East, as some obviously have done, that the decisions made should be political decisions, and that the military commanders in the field should follow those political decisions. As a matter of fact one of the things that has disturbed me in this Korean affair is that, as United Nations, we have failed to work out any effective method of controlling the military arm or the military forces assembled by the United Nations.
In our long history with these institutions that we call parliamentary, particularly in the Stuart period, and subsequently, the great struggle was as to who should control the standing army. In our parliamentary institutions we have achieved that control. It is rather different in the United States, however, where the president as commander in chief has great personal power. In our institutions nothing can be done without the actual and prior collective consent of the cabinet and of the parliamentary institution concerned.
I have been much disturbed about the lack of control of the military forces by civilian authority. At the moment we are setting up a western European force, and we are contributing to it. If I may just digress to this extent, I would say that one of the problems we should be thinking through carefully is how we are going to maintain effective civilian control of the armed forces that are being established in western Europe. I believe all the peoples of the democracies have confidence in General Eisenhower. I believe he is looked upon as being a wise man, a brilliant general, and a very human individual. But General Eisenhower may be removed; he is human. Anything may happen, and in such circumstances we do not know who would replace him. It could be someone in whom we would not have the confidence we have in General Eisenhower. And even with him, ways and means must be devised by the nations to retain control of the armed forces where that control should lie, and that is in the civilian arm of government.
The military have their tactical decisions to make after the civilian arm has laid down the objectives. I suggest that was the whole point in my hon. friend's remarks as to whether the 38th parallel is the actual place to stop. I believe it is. Whether there is a better defensive position just below or just beyond the parallel is a question, again, which should be referred to the United Nations which, in turn, would take the advice

of its military advisers and reach a decision -not by Washington, not by General Mac-Arthur, but by the United Nations, acting under instructions from their governments in unison.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTION AS TO RECROSSING OF 38TH PARALLEL BY UNITED NATIONS TROOPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house
will be glad to know that I have no intention of fighting General MacArthur's war either in Ottawa or at Lake Success. Like the hon. gentleman who has just sat down I also had the honour once of serving in the ranks. At that time I felt that I could probably fight more effectively than some of the generals in the field of strategy, but I have since learned better.
The question that is in our minds, the question that has been brought up this afternoon, is not, as has been pointed out, entirely a military question. While it certainly has military significance, it is political as well. It is a question, if I may put it that way, of whether to cross or not to
'Mr. Gillis.]
cross the 38th parallel. More accurately it is a question of whether to recross or not to recross the 38th parallel.
There is a real difficulty from my point of view in dealing with this matter because at. this moment, even this afternoon, informal discussions are going on in Washington with the other countries participating in the Korean campaign on the subject of what would be a proper political directive, if a directive should be issued, for the United Nations commander in Korea on this matter.
Although I do not think the United Nations has any right to fight General MacArthur's war, nevertheless it is our duty as members of the United Nations to lay down the political directives which would govern his operations. He is the first one to accept that fact. This question has come up before. As hon. members know, it came up last October when we were at the United Nations assembly. We then took a decision which authorized General MacArthur to use his own judgment whether to cross this particular line or not to cross it. We certainly have no right to complain of the decision although I think it is true to say that one of the factors in a good many minds at that time leading up to the United Nations resolution was the hope, indeed the expectation, that the crossing of this line might not result in a rush for the Manchurian or Russian border. I am not disposed to criticize that decision by virtue of hindsight because it might have been a very tempting idea at that time to clean up the war completely. It did not work out that way.
The discussions we are having now in Washington with the participating powers are concerned with this question once again. They are informal discussions, as any formal decision, or indeed any formal discussion will have to take place at the United Nations. But I think it is helpful for these countries which are participating in Korea to exchange views on this matter at this time, and that is what is going on. I do not think it is desirable for me to express any particular policy in regard to this matter at this time so far as Canada is concerned, for the reasons which have been indicated by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis).
It certainly would be unwise and unfair to the commander and to the men in the field to tell the enemy exactly what we were going to do in a military way when we reached that particular line. I think that that certainly would be playing into the hands of those whom we do not wish to help. No doubt when the decision is taken it will be governed by both military and political considerations. From the military

point of view, the first responsibility of the United Nations to its commander and to its forces is not to prevent him from taking action which he may consider it necessary to take to safeguard his men. I am sure that none of us would wish to do that.
It may be possible, or it may not, for a certain type of military action to be taken which might involve the tactical crossing of a particular line or the withdrawal from that line. It is that kind of decision which has to be made and, with all respect, I do not think it can be made at this time as the result of anything I may say in, this house.
Although military considerations are important, political considerations are equally important, possibly more important. When a decision was taken last October to authorize the United Nations commander to cross this line if he saw fit, there were political reasons behind that decision as well as military. The political reasons were that the United Nations felt that it should authorize necessary action to liberate and unify all of Korea. That is what we hoped would happen as a result of that decision, but unfortunately it did not happen.
I think most of us saw in our minds at that time certain dangers in that decision. Those dangers turned out to be much greater than we had realized. Possibly we were wrong in not realizing that. Well, we are up against the same kind of situation now and at least we have the advantage of experience. I hope that this time we will take all the factors into consideration so that the decision will be both militarily and politically wise.
It looks at the present time as if the situation in Korea may result in what General Ridgway, the United Nations commander in Korea, has called a military stalemate. He made that statement the other day and it was received with great interest in a number of countries. I myself would prefer to think of the situation, not so much as a military stalemate but as a stabilization of the military position. We might even reach a position where we have a sort of de facto cease-fire. What do we do then? All I would say on that point, Mr. Speaker, is that if we do reach the position of a sort of de facto cease-fire roughly along the line of the 38th parallel I think we should take advantage of that position, that military stabilization, to reopen negotiations with the people on the other side provided there is any possibility of that being brought about- and I have no illusions as to the difficulties on that score.
But if this position is to be stabilized in a way which now seems possible, it would
Korea
surely be statesmanlike to take advantage of that position to see if we can work out the kind of settlement which will make it possible for us to extricate ourselves, as the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) has said, "with honour", from Korea, because Korea is not the main danger front. For that purpose it might be desirable to try to negotiate something along the lines of the six point proposal which was put forward by our own delegation at Lake Success after consultation with a good many other delegations. I know that that idea is in the minds of people now, and I hope that possibly we might be able to utilize a favourable military situation to bring about a favourable political situation. But there again we must never forget that it takes two to make peace although it sometimes takes only one to make war.
We have not very much ground for optimism that the Chinese communist government will meet us more than halfway in any effort of this kind. However, I hope that the opportunity may present itself, and that we may be able to work out some kind of solution which will make it possible to bring this horrible conflict in Korea to an end with honour to ourselves and with freedom and unity to the Korean people. As General Ridgway pointed out, it is not the obligation of the United Nations to unify Korea by force, but it is our obligation to do everything we can to bring about that unity. I should think that the best way in which it could be done would be by negotiation if that is possible.
The good offices committee of the United Nations has already taken action in this direction. It has made an approach to the government in Peking but it has received no reply whatever to that approach. I would think that it would be unwise for us to despair because of that fact. There may be other avenues of approach; there may be other ways in which this can be done. We should certainly, I feel, use every possible opportunity to exploit every military advantage to achieve a political result which will end this conflict. If we can do that the objective of the United Nations in Korea will have been achieved, and something may have been gained out of the horrible carnage that has gone on there because it will at least have shown that the United Nations can act effectively on the battlefield and in the council chamber.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) has said that we should use the experience we have gained in the Korean operation to work out a system of control under the North Atlantic organization by which the military is brought under appropriate international civilian control, the kind of control we take for granted in our own

Supply-Health and Welfare country. There has been difficulty about this in Korea but I would point out to those who emphasize the difficulty-and at times it is a difficulty which leads to some exasperation -that its basis is the fact that in the United Nations Korean operation about 95 per cent of the actual fighting in the field has been done by the forces of one country. Naturally the government of that country is going to exercise a preponderating influence in that operation, and we should be the last to criticize that. I think that on the whole we have very little to complain about the consultation which we have managed to achieve at Lake Success and in Washington on this matter.
The translation of the results of that consultation to the commanders across the Pacific is not always as effective or as easy as we would like it to be, but I suggest that is largely because of the nature of the operation. We are working along different lines in the North Atlantic organization and we are building up not only a military organization which will be effective, we hope, in preventing war, but a political organization which will be able to control, as civilian governments should control, the military arm. I think that is all that I should say now, Mr. Speaker, but I should like to repeat once again that as we approach a decision on this matter in Korea -and we are approaching that-I hope that decision will be both politically and militarily wise.

Under this item for food and drugs, I may say that the Minister of National Health and Welfare will recall that some days ago I drew to his attention a report appearing in the Montreal Gazette which indicated that a prominent nutritionist in Montreal has stated that a good deal of the brown bread offered for sale is not whole wheat bread but is simply bread made of white flour and dyed brown by the use of molasses or other ingredients. I asked the minister if he would look into the matter, and the next day he made a statement in the house. As I recall that statement, without turning it up in Hansard, the minister said that under the Food and Drugs Act there are regulations which stipulate that if a baker puts out bread which he chooses to call Canada approved vitamin B bread, it must contain a stipulated percentage of whole wheat flour. However, he said a baker not wishing to use that label, not wishing to say it was Canada approved or vitamin B bread, came under no such regulations. This means, for example, that when unwrapped brown bread is put on the market the public has no way of knowing for sure whether it is whole wheat bread or whether it is, as the Montreal nutritionist described it, white bread dyed brown.

My purpose in raising the matter again at this time is to inquire whether consideration has been given to amending the regulations under the Food and Drugs Act so as to take care of this situation. I can tell the minister from the correspondence I have had that there is a considerable amount of interest in the matter. I find that a good many people are amazed to find that any brown bread, by virtue of being brown, would not be made from whole wheat flour. It does seem to me that the whole purpose of the act and the regulations under it is to protect people in these matters, and that a regulation governing this matter would be quite in order. I want to make it perfectly clear that there is no suggestion that any of this dyed bread fails to meet the health requirements; no suggestion is made that the ingredients used to dye it brown are not proper ingredients for human consumption. The point is that people generally assume that if bread is brown, it is whole wheat and has a certain vitamin B content. It appears now there is no guarantee of this; so my question is whether consideration will be given to amending the regulations to take care of this matter.

This is an item, Mr. Chairman, on which there has been considerable discussion. I rise to move that a sum of $65 million be voted to take care of the announcement made by the Prime Minister on March 2 that this house would be asked to provide that sum to be paid the wheat board for distribution to the farmers under the five-year pool. The question has been raised as to why the payment should be made. The government has agreed that the farmers had a right to expect a payment. That is the reason for the payment being proposed.
Had a right?

The government has agreed that the farmers had a right to expect a payment. The United Kingdom government took the position that they did not agree they were further obligated. They have been informed

Supply-Agriculture
from time to time that, although we must accept their decision, many of us in Canada would of necessity feel differently.

I shall give you this, and then you can ask your questions afterwards.

The documents were tabled,
and they did not indicate anything of this nature.
If my hon. friend thinks he is going to tell me what speech I am going to deliver in this house, he had better think again.
I am telling you what the facts are.

You can tell me the facts when I sit down, if you know what they are.
The United Kingdom government took the position that they did not agree they were further obligated. They have been informed from time to time that, although we must accept their decision, many of us in Canada would of necessity feel differently. We delayed taking action until they had been given every opportunity to change their position. I do not believe we can improve matters by discussing further the question of differences, although I am quite prepared to discuss them if my hon. friends want to have a discussion along that line.
The fact is that it was suggested in December, 1948, that a reasonable settlement of the "have regard to" clause would be made if the United Kingdom government would pay $100 million into the five-year pool. We estimated that the agreement entered into in January of 1949, to be applied to the sale to Britain of 140 million bushels in the fourth year of the contract, could have adjusted the amount by $35 million leaving $65 million to be met.
The question has been asked from time to time how we arrived at the figure of $65 million as related to the loan. Shortly after Sir Stafford Cripps began his drive to improve the dollar reserves of the United Kingdom, it was made apparent that this policy was going to be driven to a successful conclusion by eliminating every claim which could not be legally established. This brought on rather constant discussion of the "have regard to" clause in the wheat agreement. The matter came up first in December of 1947

when the British delegation on finance was in Ottawa; again in September of 1948 when Sir Stafford Cripps was in Ottawa; and finally in London in December of 1948 when I was there. After each of these discussions 1 raised the question with my colleagues as to how our claims under the "have regard to" clause could be safeguarded, and suggested holding back $100 million of the loan so that the dollar position could not be made a reason for not meeting the claim. It was explained to me on each occasion that the lack of a legal claim could make it difficult to make part of the loan available unless by mutual agreement.
When the special agreement was entered into in January of 1949, providing for a possible settlement of $35 million, I reduced my suggested caveat on the loan to $65 million. In June, 1950, shortly after the May 22 discussions, other justifiable reasons existed for reaching mutual agreement that no further amounts would be utilized from the loan excepting with Canada's consent. Unfortunately the United Kingdom took the position that the dollar reserve account would be affected by a loan in much the same manner as by paying cash, and could not be persuaded to use the remainder of the loan for the purpose suggested.
I am sure it will be understood that it could not be agreed that any arrangement entered into with Canadian farmers in 1946 could be set aside indefinitely because of dollar difficulties in the United Kingdom. When it was decided by the United Kingdom on May 22, 1950, that they were not paying more we felt we had to accept that as the legal position, and after every possible means of inducing them to reconsider their decision had been exhausted, we decided that the wheat farmer should not bear the burden of the decision alone, but that the amount we had asked the United Kingdom to pay should be taken out of the consolidated revenue fund in the financial year 1950-51 and paid into the wheat pool to be distributed as soon as possible. I use the words "wheat pool" there not in the sense that it is to be paid to the wheat pools of the different provinces but to the five-year pool that was set up under the wheat board.
We have been asked how we arrived at the figure of $100 million as a reasonable settlement for the years 1946-47, rather than $350 million as suggested by advocates of the grain exchange marketing system. We checked the method by which the grain exchange and others arrived at this figure of $350 million. I suppose it is not necessary for me to put the plan on Hansard because it has been put there a number of times by the member for

Souris (Mr. Ross), and by others-I believe almost the exact figures that I am going to place on Hansard now. We took the agreement figures of the sales to Britain from the 1946 crop, which amounted to 160 million bushels, and found that on the basis of class II prices of $2.43 No. 1 northern Fort William being the world price, the difference between that and $1.55 is 88 cents or a total of $140 million. Then we took the agreement figures of sales to Britain from the 1947 crop, which amounted to 160 million bushels, and found that on the basis of class II prices of $2.88 No. 1 northern Fort William being the world price, the difference between that and $1.55 is $1.33 or a total of $212,800,000. This gives a grand total of $352,800,000, and that is the figure which has been used by all critics of this plan from the time it was first set up until the time the actual figures have become known.
But I maintain that the class II price is not a proper basis to take, first because only 89 million bushels were sold in small quantities to different countries, to many markets, and second because the entire profit of the speculative market of the United States is represented in the build-up of that price. The speculative profit would not go to the farmers and hence should not be charged to the British. This was when we were making our representations to the British at the different times I have indicated earlier in what I had to say.
In order to find a price which would only apply to farmers in a similar area, I went to the agricultural department of the United States and secured the average price received by farmers at their local points for wheat each year. I found that the difference between the average the United States farmer received and what the Canadian farmer received for his 1946 crop was not 88 cents but 33 cents. This on the contract sale of 160 million bushels to Great Britain in 1946 would be $52,800,000. The difference between the average the United States farmer would receive and what the Canadian farmer would receive for his 1947 crop was not $1.33 on the basis used by exchange critics, but 71 cents. The Minister of Agriculture has sought to re-emphasize in the house the impression that the government of the United Kingdom did not make the payments it should have made. That is the basic difference between the points of view put forward by two ministers, which is of the utmost importance in dealing

with the payment now before the parliament of Canada, and for which the government is asking approval.
On Thursday last, as sessional paper 113-A, the records of the meeting of May 22 of last year in London were placed upon the table, and also a copy of the message sent to the government of the United Kingdom on May 30. These records do not leave any impression that the government of Canada was simply recognizing the declaration by the government of the United Kingdom that nothing further was owing. On the contrary these make it perfectly clear that, as of May 30 of last year, the government of Canada in a formal declaration, communicated through official channels, agreed with the government of the United Kingdom that nothing further was owing.
There is a very great difference between those two positions. What is more, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) went to some pains in the house a week ago Monday to make it perfectly clear that in his opinion the government of the United Kingdom had fulfilled its part of the contract in every way. What is more, he finished his remarks by deploring the fact that anyone should suggest that the government of the United Kingdom had not played fair with the government and people of Canada.
Those two positions cannot go hand in hand. Those two positions have a profound effect upon the subject we are now considering. If there was in fact a belief on, the part of the government of Canada that there was some balance owing in respect of the contract, then it might be natural that the government would say, "We entered into a contract believing it would be setting up a certain basis, and we are going to make good the difference between what we think should have been done and what actually was done."
But that is not the position of the government. By their agreement on May 30 last year that the government of the United Kingdom had carried out its obligation in full, they denied the possibility that they can now assert as a government that there was any balance owing under that contract. Therefore the payment now proposed by the government must be on some other basis-and we-are still waiting to be told what that basis is..
Since the government by its own decision of May 30 last year cannot possibly ask the House of Commons now to approve of a payment in respect of a contract which had been fully paid, then they must ask us to approve of this under some other principle, and upon some other basis.
In the earlier discussions on the subject it was pointed out that there might be

Supply-Agriculture
another basis. When the government takes over wheat, or any agricultural product -or in fact any product of any kind, or any personal service-by compulsion, then unquestionably there is a moral obligation on the part of the government to reimburse those whose products or services are being taken under compulsion, and to reimburse them on a just and proper basis. If that is the basis then we are still waiting to be told that that is the principle under which the payment is to be made. What we have pointed out is that if such principle is enunciated in this house then obviously that principle must apply with equal force to every other agricultural producer, to the hog raiser, to the fruit grower, to the potato grower, to the dairy producer, to everyone else whose products are taken over under the compulsion that goes with the emergency powers now possessed by the government. The same principle would apply with equal force to production of every kind and to personal services as well.
It has been made abundantly clear that in this house there is a desire to make sure that people in every part of this country are dealt with fairly and properly and justly wherever the government takes action that denies to the individual the right to assert his own position as to what he shall receive for his product or for his services. The explanation given today for the manner in which the $65 million was determined as the figure to be paid does not show any mathematical basis for the calculation of that amount. The obvious fact is that there was $65 million still unclaimed of the loan made available to the government of the United Kingdom. Whether we use the euphonious expression that it was pointed out to the government of the United Kingdom that there was $65 million available for this purpose, or whether we say that it was suggested to the government of the United Kingdom that they should pay $65 million as the balance under this contract by taking up the remainder of the loan and then paying it over to the government, the fact is that the figure of $65 million was arrived at in that way. No other basis of computation has been put forward as yet.

This is a matter which affects all Canadians. I am sure that people in every part of this country will recognize that payment made upon any other basis would only leave a most unsatisfactory situation in which there would be no clear understanding as to how similar obligations would be dealt with in the future. Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words in connection with this bill. I would call attention to a heading which appeared in a newspaper and which I feel is perhaps applicable to some who, as yet, have not seen the advantage in our endeavour not only to build up British Columbia but to build Canada as a whole. This article bears a Massachusetts dateline, but I believe it would apply elsewhere. The heading is, "774 Vote for Man Dead Two Weeks". It struck me that this might apply to those who as yet have not realized that there is such a thing as the province of British Columbia, and who do not know just how worth while it is to build up that province, thereby improving the entire economy of Canada, and particularly that of Alberta.
In the last couple of years some of us have been accused of conducting a filibuster. This is what the Vancouver Sun of March 15 has to say on the subject:
Filibuster Without Guns
British Columbia members of parliament are fighting in Commons to guarantee an oil industry in this province. And they rightly object to their struggle being dubbed a "filibuster."
They want parliament to make sure that any oil pipe line from Alberta to the coast is routed through B.C. and Vancouver so Canada will get a crack at the oil1 flow before U.S. does. They're opposed to incorporating any company that would skip B.C. to enter the U.S. through southern Alberta.
If it takes a hundred speeches to pound home the legitimate economic interests of B.C. that still isn't a "filibuster."
And, mark you, this is the Vancouver Sun; this is not a section of the press that believes in the building up of British Columbia only.
The word nowadays means "organized obstruction tactics by dilatory motions or artifices."
Perhaps B.C. members should use the word against supporters of U.S. routes. They could remind parliament that originally a filibuster was an armed raid against a peaceful country to secure loot. They could argue that companies which propose to pipe Canadian oil first to Seattle and Portland just lack the guns.

Vancouver got an Indication this week of what a pipe line from Edmonton oilfields through the Yellowhead pass to this city could mean. British American Oil Company announced it would build a $10 million refinery here.
And may I add that if hon. members were to check Hansard they would find that that is exactly what those of us who have been fighting this battle for two years have been saying. This $10 million is just a beginning in the development of our province. It is unfortunate that this heading had not appeared earlier.
It might be too expensive to supply such a plant by tanker from Seattle or Portland.
The Yellowhead route also opens tremendous prospects for the development of B.C.'s Peace river oilfields.
This is of particular significance to some, so I shall repeat it:
The Yellowhead route also opens tremendous prospects for the development of B.C.'s Peace river oilfields. A major discovery there could be drained off by a feeder line running due south to join the main line in central B.C. That couldn't be done if the main line ran through Alberta.
Nor have parliamentary supporters of the U.S. route backed up their claim that a line running 400 miles south through Alberta then swinging west to the coast would be cheaper than an all-B.C. line. The B.C. route follows the C.N.R.'s easy grade over the Rockies for a direct 750 miles to Vancouver.
Though parliament hasn't the power to fix actual routes, it needn't encourage any route that skips B.C. It needn't incorporate any company proposing a U.S. route when already incorporated companies are pledged to B.C. pipe lines.
And all M.P.'s should remember that Vancouver is the west coast port of Canada as well as of B.C.
I am very pleased to have taken part in the development set out in this editorial, and to have had associated with me other members from British Columbia. I know hon. members from other provinces who in the last two years came to our aid will pardon me if I do not make reference to them. Time does not permit me to cover the ground in full- because this is one of the bills I want to see passed tonight.

Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line they also raise fruit. Then, from the famous Okanagan, the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Jones) came to our help. Mr. Speaker, this is a bill that was passed by the Senate after going through their committee on private bills. It also has had the approval of the Secretary of State and the commissioner of patents. However, I want to explain the purpose of the bill. It is simply to validate a patent application filed in the Canadian patent office by one George Hanks, on July 16, 1947. In 1947, as hon. members will recall, parliament passed certain amendments to the Patent Act. One of them had as its purpose to permit the filing of patent applications in Canada by nationals of countries which accord reciprocal privileges where the normal time within which such applications should have been filed had expired during the war years.
Section 28A stipulated two conditions, however, attached to the receiving of such patent applications by the commissioner of patents. First, such applications had to be filed not later than the 15th day of November, 1947. Second, the application for a patent had to request the commissioner of patents to extend the time by special request. In the case of George Hanks the facts are these. He applied for and obtained a patent on his invention in the United States patent office under date of April 23, 1946. Since he had filed more than a year before that date in the United States, and since he had not filed his application in Canada before the issue of the United States patent, under our law he was forbidden to file an application in this country and obtain a patent.
After the legislation was passed in 1947 George Hanks through his attorneys requested that he be allowed to file an application in Canada. The attorneys filed before November of 1947 but through some mistake they did not accompany the application with a so-called formal request to come under section 28A. The bill would now allow George Hanks to have the right to validate his application in Canada in spite of the fact that there was not this so-called formal letter requesting that he be given the advantages of section 28A. As I said before, the commissioner of patents and the Secretary of State have approved. My purpose is to ask that the bill be allowed to pass so that it may be sent to the standing committee on private bills.

576. To authorize and provide for a payment to the Canadian wheat board which shall be dealt with by the board in all respects as though it was

money received from the sale of wheat produced in the designated area, sold and delivered to the board by producers during the pool period commencing on the first day of August, 1945, and ending on the thirty-first day of July, 1950, and to authorize the board, notwithstanding the provisions of subsections 2 and 3 of section 22 of the Canadian Wheat Board Act, to distribute such amount together with all other moneys received by the board from the sale of such wheat, after making the deductions provided for in the said section 22, among holders of certificates issued by the board pursuant to part III of the said act during the pool period aforesaid, by paying to the person named in such certificate the same sum for each bushel of wheat referred to therein, $65,000,000.

The subject under consideration is item 576. The subject matter of this item has been discussed in the house for the past two or three weeks and I do not intend to take much time. As a matter of fact, this is the first time I have discussed the subject. I have been a good listener, and I have tried to find some grains of wheat among all the chaff that has been blown about the house in the past ten days or two weeks.
This item has to do with the payment of $65 million to the western wheat growers. It is based on the wheat contract between Great Britain and Canada over a period of years. We all know that a contract is something which people more or less consider to be inviolate; and we expect all parties under a contract to live up to its conditions and its terms. If that contract has not been carried out by one party, we expect that that party should be made to carry out its terms. I might say at the outset that I have every respect for the grain growers of the west. I feel as do all people from my part of the country. If there is anything coming to the farmers of western Canada, we would be anxious to see them have it. As a matter of fact, to a great extent western Canada is made up of people from the maritimes. We have always, at all times, wished them well; and we still wish them well. If at times, such as at the time of the Red river flood, they need assistance, the people in eastern Canada will be most anxious to send what help they can. The same was true some years ago when they suffered from burnt-out areas. People from all parts of Canada were pleased indeed to send what aid they could to help the people in the west.
As I said a moment ago, if the grain growers are entitled to something under the contract, we would be in favour of passing the item. We know that wheat is our greatest exportable commodity; its export is the lifeblood of the country. It is responsible for the prosperity of the people in the west. If they are not prosperous the people in other parts of Canada are not prosperous either.

There is another point which I say that we as representatives of the people must take into consideration. We must ask ourselves what responsibility we have to our constituents. If this $65 million is to be paid-and it is a very large amount-people in my province and in other sections of Canada will have certain questions to ask their members. I know I will be asked: Why was it paid? Why did we pay $65 million to western Canada? Was it because the contract with the British people had not been lived up to? We can only quote what has been quoted so often in the house, namely the words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, when he said that he deplored the suggestion that the British government had not played fair with the Canadian people. We have had tabled in the house a document which shows that the British government did play fair with Canada.
Well, if that is so, they must have played fair with the Canadian government and with the grain growers of western Canada- because these are all Canadian people. So when we are asked if there is any legal right to the payment of this $65 million, I do not think that, in the face of the facts and in the face of statements made and documents tabled in the house, we can say anything other than there is no legal obligation under the contract to pay any money to western Canada.
Another question our people would be justified in asking would be this: Are we morally bound? Is there any moral reason for our paying out this large sum of money to the grain growers of western Canada? As I said a moment ago, a contract is a contract. If it has been legally carried out, then it has been morally carried out. People are making contracts continuously, and when minds meet and a contract has been legally carried out, then to my mind there is no argument which would support any suggestion that it has not been morally carried out.
The third question which I believe our people would ask is this: Did the farmers of western Canada suffer because of this British wheat agreement? Did they have to sell their wheat below the cost of production, as the people in New Brunswick have had to sell their potatoes? We have been told by the Minister of Agriculture himself that he considers it a good contract. We have been told the same thing by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. No one in the house has suggested that the western farmers sold below cost of production. It is agreed that they got a price which was much higher than their cost of production, and I am told that during the term of the contract there was prosperity in the west.

Having disposed of the questions which might be asked by our constituents-whether it was legal, whether there was any moral obligation and whether the farmers have suffered-we will then be asked: Why are we paying $65 million to the grain growers of western Canada? If we reply by using the argument used in the house we would have to say that the western farmer was led to expect certain things, that expectations were raised in his mind, and that it is those expectations which form the basis upon which we are paying this large sum of money to the western grain growers.
I remember having read some years ago the book "Great Expectations". I am sure most hon. members have read that book by Charles Dickens and have seen the motion picture of the same name. As I recall, one of the characters in the book, a small boy, had assisted a felon who had escaped from justice, and the assistance had been given under compulsion. In later years the boy began to receive money from some source, although he did not know just where it was coming from. He was sent to a good boarding school, given money to spend and trained to be a gentleman. The money kept coming in constantly, and the young gentleman thought it was being sent to him by people having great influence and wealth.
One day however he found out who his benefactor was, it was disclosed to him that his benefactor all those years had been the felon who had escaped from justice, who had gone to Australia and made a fortune and who, as he thought, was repaying the boy for the help he had received in the past.
That is the story of "Great Expectations". I wonder if the expectations of the farmers in western Canada were raised on a somewhat similar basis; I wonder whether it was for past favours the government had received, or for future benefits it hoped to get. In any event we can have our own ideas in that connection.

In connection with these expectations we have heard that they were raised more or less by the Hon. Mr. Strachey, the British minister of food, when he made a speech in Winnipeg. I have heard of the $64 question but I never heard before of a $65 million speech. That is what they are accusing Mr. Strachey of having made in Winnipeg. In fact, some people would have us believe that it was a $300 million or $400 million speech.
Mr. Strachey did make a speech in Winnipeg which the Minister of Agriculture quoted when he was speaking a few days ago, but

he left out what I considered was the most important part of that speech. Mr. Strachey said:
I repeat that the essence of the agreement-
This is the part which I contend the Minister of Agriculture left out.
-is that in return for selling wheat at $1.55 during the first two years of the agreement, Canadian farmers get the protection of minimum floor prices of $1.25 and $1 in the third and fourth years. And I reiterate that it is an inescapable obligation of the British government to pay at least these prices however low the world price of wheat may go.
That was the essence of the agreement which was made, according to Mr. Strachey. The Minister of Agriculture will remember that in 1947 it was mentioned in this house and in the country that there was a great possibility of deflation. Our own government, and probably the government of Great Britain, thought that the price of wheat might go below $1.25 and $1. The British government guaranteed that no matter how low the price went they would live up to their agreement and would put on a floor price of $1.25 and $1 per bushel.
A lot has been made of the "have regard to" clause but so far I have not heard a proper definition of that clause given in this house. I think it can be taken for granted that one thing that was meant was that if the world price of wheat went up instead of going down, as the Minister of Agriculture expected it would, having regard to that the British government were willing to pay and did pay $2 per bushel for wheat. They did not say that they were going to pay the world price and that evidently was not demanded from the British, but they were asked to pay $2 per bushel for wheat and that is the price they paid. I submit that that is what was meant by the "have regard to" clause. They were having regard to the price of wheat going up and upped their price as stated.
I am not here to defend the British government, but as was stated the other day, Great Britain has built up trade in this country over a hundred years by honouring her contracts and by the excellence of her products. Great Britain became the greatest trader in the world and it little behooves us to try to blame that country, which has had such a long history of honour and integrity. Some people say it is the socialist government. I am not a socialist and I would like to see the socialist government beaten when they go to the country.
I have read the life of Mr. Attlee and I believe he is an honest and honourable man.
I think all hon. members will agree with me in that. Mr. Ernest Bevin is respected and honoured by his own people and by democratic people throughout the world. So

is Mr. Morrison. All these men are honourable men and I say it is unfair and unjust and untrue to say that such men would dishonour their contract.
The questions which I mentioned a few moments ago will be asked me by people in New Brunswick. I say to the Minister of Agriculture that if farmers in any part of Canada are suffering or have suffered during the last five years it is the farmers of the maritime provinces, particularly the potato growers. I am not using this as a quid pro quo argument, that because we are giving $65 million to the western farmers we must give it to the eastern farmers, but I do want to say that these people are getting hardly fifty per cent of the cost of production of the commodity they produce and yet they are being asked to help to pay this $65 million to the farmers of western Canada.
A few days ago the Turgeon committee after a most cursory investigation reported that the Chignecto canal was not feasible. We believe that it is. Sixty-five million dollars would have built the Chignecto canal which would have been of lasting benefit to the people in our part of the country. It will be pretty difficult for me or anyone else to go into my part of Canada and justify something for which there is no legal or moral ground as far as the records of this house are concerned and at the same time support this item for $65 million.
It is not my intention to take any more time of the committee. As my leader stated this afternoon, if instead of quoting a lot of confusing figures the Minister of Agriculture had given us some good and sound reason why this money should be paid, I and the people whom I represent would have been only too glad to agree to the fulfilling of obligations by the people of Canada and the paying of this $65 million. But when you analyse the minister's statements this afternoon and the statements which have been made in this house in the past two weeks I can see no just reason why the people of Canada should pay $65 million to the western wheat growers and I for one am opposed to this item.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to move:
That item 576 of the further supplementary estimates be reduced from $65,000,000 to $1.
In moving this motion I regret very much that we are in committee because it will be impossible for certain hon. members to record for posterity their opposition to this measure which, as I said before, I regard as an agrarian commando raid upon the public treasury of Canada.
