They could have sold me on that. I would have thought it would have been a much wiser way to spend $65 million. I would hope that my friends in the cabinet would say so too if they were able to express their private opinions on this particular question.
I wish to protest on behalf of every taxpayer in Canada against what I believe to be an unwarranted and painful operation on the pocketbook of every taxpayer in Canada. I invite every member of the house to assist the country in saving $64,999,999 for the Canadian taxpayers. At the same time I think that anybody who votes for this motion will administer a rebuke to the government which in this case I believe they have coming to them. I hope that as a result of our actions we will deter the government from any step of a like nature in the future.

I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that the few remarks I have to make will take very little time but I do want to put on record tonight the position of the eastern wheat grower. It is quite apparent that the government intends to put through this $65

million, regardless of whether it is sufficient or insufficient. It is an amount which they grabbed out of the air and nothing has been said in the house yet to verify whether it is correct or not so far as the losses to the western farmers are concerned. As a matter of fact, the government, through the Prime Minister and the Minister of Trade and Commerce, have never admitted that loss to the farmers through the wheat contract. The Prime Minister admits, however, that the western farmer is disappointed that he did not get more from that wheat contract. The amount of $65 million is simply grabbed out of the air and it is said to be the amount to be paid to them.
Is it that this amount has been taken to satisfy election promises or to save the hide of the Minister of Agriculture in the western provinces?
This afternoon the Minister of Agriculture showed a small sign of arrogance and admitted his error when in effect he stated that the Minister of Trade and Commerce and he himself could make statements which may not be correct because they have a leader who can iron out their differences. That is a terrific admission for the Minister of Agriculture to make.
I just want to point out the grave injustice to the eastern wheat growers, as admitted by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in report No. 4 of the agriculture and colonization committee at page 108, of Wednesday, June 7, 1950. I shall quote from the report:

The eastern farmer in the years
1945, 1946 and 1947 took $1.25 for his wheat, when the western farmer was getting $1.75, so the eastern farmer took a beating.

He was free to sell it
where he liked.

Yes, that is true, but at a stated
price.

Yes. Almost everybody
was put under a ceiling at that time but the eastern farmer was not. So far as pegged prices go, everything which the farmer bought was at a pegged price, under November, 1941, prices yet his wheat was allowed to go up.
There was an interjection by Mr. Wright which I do not think is necessary or relevant, and then my question goes on:
By Mr. Charlton:
Q. Yes, but not nearly up to $1.75.-A. No.

I always thought that the eastern producer got trimmed in that period.
That is an admission made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce himself. He said that he thought the eastern farmer took a trimming during that period in which the wheat board was in effect handling eastern wheat.	[DOT]
Then on March 6 of this year I asked the Prime Minister a question on the orders of 80709-94
Supply-Agriculture
the day which is to be found on page 947 of Hansard, and reads as follows:

Mr. Speaker, in view of the announced policy of the government by the Prime Minister to subsidize wheat producers for losses incurred under the wheat agreement, has the government given consideration to the position of the eastern wheat growers, cheese producers, hog producers and apple growers whose products were sold below world prices under government contract to the United Kingdom?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the answer is no.
To be fair I think I should go on and quote the supplementary question and the answer to it, which are found on the next page:

In view of the short answer given
by the Prime Minister to my question, may I ask, if the government has not already considered the matter, whether it is prepared to do so now?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We are always prepared to consider anything, but that does not mean that the results of the consideration would be something that would comply with the apparent hopes behind the hon. member's question.
It took 33 words to say the same thing as the answer to the first question.
In report No. 5 of the committee on agriculture and colonization, dated June 8, 1950, we find a fairly concise report of what the eastern situation really is. The discussion started- on page 125 of that report. A question was asked regarding the handling of eastern wheat by the wheat board, and the witness said that he could get the information. I will quote what he said:
The Witness: This is contained in our report for the year 1946-47.
Ontario Winter Wheat.
From August 1, 1939, to July 31, 1944, board operations in Canada eastern winter wheat were governed by the terms of the Canadian Wheat Board Act 1935.
In the crop year 1941-42 the board was relieved of the responsibility of purchasing Canada eastern winter wheat unless the market price fell to support levels. This policy continued through the crop years 1942-43 and 1943-44.
Changed circumstances brought about a new government policy with respect to Ontario winter wheat in the crop year 1944-45, the main features of which were:
(1)	The board was exempted from its obligations under section 14 of the Canadian Wheat Board Act;
(2)	The board was charged with maintaining a floor price of $1.25 per bushel for top grades of Canada eastern winter wheat, basis delivered Montreal;
(3)	The Ontario wheat equalization fund was established and it became the responsibility of the board to assess equalization fees against Ontario wheat and wheat products sold for export.
The board did not have to purchase wheat in support of floor prices on Ontario wheat, but fees collected in connection with the equalization fund resulted in a surplus of $188,226.09 which was distributed to producers.
The 1944-45 Ontario wheat policy was continued in the crop year 1945-46. Again no action was necessary by the board in support of floor prices. The equalization fund amounted to $262,114.91 and was distributed to producers.

Supply-Agriculture
Government policy with respect to Ontario winter wheat during the crop year 1946-47 included several major changes and was as follows:
(1)	The Board was charged with the responsibility of maintaining a floor price of $1.25 per bushel for No. 1 Canada eastern winter wheat basis delivered Montreal;
(2)	The maximum price of $1.26 per bushel for Canada eastern winter wheat basis delivered Montreal, established in 1941 was continued;
(3)	Equalization fees on exports of Ontario winter wheat and wheat flour were continued;
(4)	The board was directed to administer a treasury payment of 9 cents per bushel over and above the maximum price for deliveries of Ontario winter wheat;
(5)	The board was directed to administer the payment to producers, at time of delivery, of a fixed and final equalization payment of 5 cents per bushel.
In administering this program the board received the full co-operation of the private trade in Ontario. Grain dealers and millers became the agents of the board in distributing the 5 cents equalization payment and the 9 cent treasury payment. They made both payments to producers at the time of delivery and were later reimbursed by the board. Wheat equalization payments amounted to $207,336.23 and treasury payments amounted to $373,207.11 on total reported marketings of 4,146,738 bushels.
Equalization fees collected on Ontario wheat and flour exported during the crop year amounted to $290,134.82, and exceeded equalization payments to producers by $82,798.59, which amount was credited to the dominion government. The net cost of the 1946-47 Ontario wheat operation to the dominion government including the treasury payment and administrative and other expenses, was $309,025.52. Financial details concerning the board's Canada eastern winter wheat operation are set forth in exhibits VIII and IX of this report.
Now, a further question by myself:
Q. Just in that connection, the last paragraph in part reads "-and exceeded equalization payments to producers by $82,798.59, which amount was credited to the dominion government." That was money collected through flour sold and in excess of the amount paid to us?
A. In excess of the estimated payment which was made at the start of the year. The fund actually realized a profit of $82,798.59.
Q. Which was not distributed to the producers?
A. No.
Now, Mr. Chairman, that might seem like a very small figure, $82,798.59, but on top of this price which we were forced to accept the government still has $82,798.59 which they are holding in the dominion treasury. On the basis of these five years, eastern wheat producers in 1943-44 took $1.25 per bushel; in 1944-45, they took $1.25 plus approximately 3 cents; ini 1945-46 they took $1.25 plus 5 cents; in 1946-47 they took $1.25 plus approximately 5 cents and 9 cents. In 1948 the price was allowed to go free and we received at least $2.20 per bushel. Averaging those five years, the price worked out at $1.48 per bushel, which is 35-3 cents less than the price now guaranteed to western producers. Now, Mr. Chairman, on an ordinary basis the difference between eastern and western wheat is approximately 10 cents.

If the $65 million is paid to western producers of wheat, when there has been no loss actually proven, and I say that a loss is proven to the eastern producers, then I think this government should do something about it. On top of the loss per bushel there is still $82,798.59 in the dominion treasury which is owing to the eastern growers.

In rising to speak briefly on the motion made by the member for Comox-Alberni, I wish at the outset to say there is no one in this house who realizes more than I do how vast a country this Canada of ours is or who realizes how diversified are its interests. I further realize what a difficult country it is to govern. At the same time, I have always believed in the old adage that what is sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander. Certainly, if the wheat producers are entitled to a bonus, then so are the cheese producers of Ontario and Quebec. The producers of those two provinces have been required to furnish cheese to fill the contracts with Great Britain. For the first ten months of 1950 this cheese was sold at 11 cents less than the domestic price, and since the war it has sold for less than world market prices.
If one follows this argument to its logical conclusion, then the hog producers are also entitled to a bonus, as are the fishermen and the gold mines that are selling their gold at less than market value. I believe the ramifications of this thing are infinite. I am sure that in a few weeks he will hear arguments being used to the effect that high taxation is a method of taking wealth out of circulation, and will therefore act as a detriment to the inflationary spiral. When I was in New Zealand last November, I learned that the New Zealand government felt obliged to withhold one-third of the wool payments owing to farmers in order to curb the danger of serious inflation in that country. We, however, are deliberately placing in the hands of the farmers of the three western provinces a sum of $65 million.
It all comes back to Ontario anyway.

I do not know about that. If the western farmer were really hard up we would all have the greatest sympathy for him. I am told', however, that bank savings accounts were never higher than they are today in the western provinces. Certainly, I feel that the farmers of Ontario and Quebec have just as good a case as, or even a better case than, the farmers of the west for the $65 million. If the $65 million must be spent in the prairie provinces, why not use it to construct irrigation schemes? We have heard from all sides-

of the desperate need for more moisture in the ground in some of the western provinces. If we had an irrigation system in the western provinces-I do not believe anyone would contradict this point-it would definitely make for more diversified' agriculture. It would mean that the western provinces would not be so dependent on wheat prices, whether they be domestic, contract or world prices.
Few if any are satisfied' with the grant, and if other agricultural interests are not to receive any benefit, I have no alternative but to agree with the member for Comox-Alberni.

I am rather surprised to hear the member for Leeds make the statement he has just made. He complains about certain people who produce cheese not receiving a subsidy, and includes certain other Ontario producers. I have in my hand a statement which appeared in yesterday's Hansard, and it shows that since the beginning of the war there has been a subsidy paid on cheese amounting to $13,567,000, of which $2,732,000 went to the province of Quebec and $10,531,000 to the province of Ontario. For factory improvement there has been paid $1,330,000, $770,000 of which went to the province of Quebec and $542,000 to the province of Ontario. The subsidy on milk for Cheddar cheese totalled $14,740,000, of which $5,494,000 went to the province of Quebec and $9,350,000 to the province of Ontario. Then, for freight assistance on feed grain the total was $138,937,000, of which $51,870,000 has been paid to the province of Quebec and $50,119,000 to the province of Ontario. There are also the hog premiums, showing the subsidies which have been paid to the hog producers of Ontario. There are also the subsidies paid for maple products. Nearly all of that has been paid to the province of Ontario and the province of Quebec. I may say that this information may be found at page 1375 of Hansard of March 19, 1951. I agree with the hon. member for Brant-Went-worth when he complains of not receiving a sufficient price for the wheat which went into domestic consumption in eastern Canada here. We in western Canada are in exactly the same position. I have in my hand the 26th annual report of the Saskatchewan Co-operative Producers Limited. This report states:
The government was advised that in the final settlement of the five-year pool, which terminated on the 31st July, 1950, provision should be made for:
(1) An adjusting payment on all wheat sold for domestic consumption during the period 1st March, 1945 to 17th February, 1947.
Supply-Agriculture
That is pretty much the period which the hon. member for Brant-Wentworth was speaking about. It further states:
As pool delegates will recall, wheat used for domestic consumption was supplied by the Canadian wheat board at $1.25 per bushel, plus carrying charges, for the period 1st March, 1945, to 17th March, 1947. During this whole period all wheat for export was sold at a price substantially above this figure. In the opinion of your board the export price during this time would average probably $1.55 a bushel.
On the basis of that subsidy to the consumers of bread in Canada, we believe that there is another $48 million due to the five-year pool over and above the $65 million which the government have placed in it. I want to say that the Liberal members of the legislature in the province of Saskatchewan have made a statement in which they are urging this government to place this additional $48 million in the five-year pool, and I have not heard the Liberal members of parliament from Saskatchewan or from western Canada getting up in this House of Commons and backing that request. I have not heard the Minister of Agriculture nor the Minister of Trade and Commerce getting up and explaining why the farmers of western Canada should not be compensated to the amount of this $48 million. Before this debate closes I hope the Minister of Agriculture will give the reasons why this government is not meeting the request not only of the wheat pools but of the Saskatchewan farmers' union, the Alberta farmers' union, Liberal members of the legislature of the province of Alberta, Liberal members of the legislature of the province of Saskatchewan and in representations that have been made to them from the province of Manitoba. We think that this is a compensation which this government owes to the wheat producers in western Canada.
There is just one other point that I want to cover and it is this. Why were not the representatives of the advisory council of the wheat board called in between May 22 and May 30 when the government finally accepted the memorandum or minutes of meetings that were submitted to them from Great Britain? When the Minister of Agriculture went to Great Britain recently he took a representative over with him. But that was after they had finally accepted on May 30 the minutes or the settlement offered by the British government. The time for the government to have called in for consultation the representatives of western Canada was before those minutes were accepted. I should just like an explanation from the minister as to why we are not entitled to another $48 million payment as requested by all representatives from western Canada, and why the

Supply-Agriculture
representatives from the west were not consulted before the final agreement was made on May 30.

It was $300 million to start
with. Why do you not make up your mind?

Before I sit down, Mr. Chairman, may I add this word or two? I have not said anything with regard to the hon. member who has just spoken; I refer to the hon. member for Comox-Albemi. But if he would remember that back in 1949, when he could not sell his lumber, the wheat producers of western Canada allowed 12,500,000 bushels of wheat to be taken out of their 1949 contract in order to make $25 million available for the purchase of lumber by Great Britain, perhaps he would not have moved the motion which he has just moved. I must say that I heartily disagree with it.
No subsidy.

The hon. member for Leeds has raised a question which I had expected was going to be raised much earlier in the discussion. As a matter of fact, I have been carrying the answer in my pocket until I have almost worn it out. The statement which was made a few minutes ago, from the Hansard of March 19, is only a part of the statistics which are available in connection with the payments which have been made by the Department of Agriculture over the years from 1939 down to the present. I have in my hand a sheet which covers all of the net costs of subventions, bonuses and subsidies paid by the federal Department of Agriculture for the fiscal years 1939-40 to 1949-50. From those dates it will be noticed that there is still one year that we have been paying after that. The total amount of the payments, before there was any vote proposed for wheat, was $727 million. Of that, over $169 million went to the dairy farmers in one form of subsidy or another; $248 million of it went to the livestock producers and the greater part of that $248 million will be paid to the same persons as are producing dairy products. Then one could go on to quote the figures with regard to all the products that have been talked about. But the only other figure that I am going to use at the moment is the one having to do with apples and vegetables, including potatoes-and I must say that the potato one is the small one among these-of $30,124,000. When one recalls that there are only about 4,000 fruit growers in Nova Scotia, where they got about $21 million or rather $18 million of that amount-the $21 million would not apply until another year's payments are made-and that the province of British Columbia, with a similar number,

received up to that time some $2 million, and since then has had $2 million, one will realize that when 250,000 farmers have a subsidy of $65 million, per family the payment in every one of the other classifications, with the possible exception again of potatoes, has been higher than the payment per family in connection with any grants that have been paid to the wheat growers in connection with wheat. I give those figures in order to ease the minds of those who think that they have got to vote against this item because the people they represent did not get anything. They have all had something. In my opinion, if you take into consideration the farmers in this country from one end to the other with regard to the payments that they have received, it will be found that they have been dealt with with extreme equality, no matter what part of Canada they live in or no matter what part of agriculture they have been conducting.
May I say that I am not altogether sure that the potato growers have been dealt with as favourably as others. There has been a reason offered, one which has been explained to the house on a number of occasions. It is more difficult to find a way of subsidizing potato growers from Ottawa, to pay federal subsidies to potato growers which I presume we would have to make apply all the way across Canada, if such subsidies were produced from here, without injuring the industry itself where it is necessary for it to continue so as to provide a reasonable living to the people concerned, than it is in connection with any of the others.
However that matter is being considered; and what we have in mind in connection with it is that when we have fully dealt with it we at least have the hope that we will have established, or assisted in establishing, some method under which these potatoes can be marketed to better advantage in the years ahead, without depending upon subsidies which may cause people to produce potatoes in great quantities in some other sections of Canada, and thus destroy the market available now for those who must produce potatoes and sell them at some distance away from the farms on which they are produced, without doing injury to those people.
I thought I should say that much. There was no wish on my part to raise a discussion in the matter, because it can be discussed at any time. But facts have been asked for by members in the house. They were placed on Hansard on the 19th, and I think a study of that partial list of facts would be useful.

The minister seems to be using a more comprehensive list than

appeared in Hansard yesterday. Could we have the one he is using placed on Hansard?

I think it could be placed on Hansard. I do not believe I could, between now and the time Hansard appears in the morning, get a copy which would take in the last year. I had thought at first that I had the last year with me, but I find now that I have not.
Perhaps it could be brought tomorrow.
We could probably put it on some time tomorrow.
The minister is talking about future plans for the potato growers. What about the present year, when they are selling potatoes for a quarter of the cost of production?

I am talking about the present year and the future. As I said yesterday, the matter is under discussion for this year. I am talking about whatever may be done this year in terms of what might be done in the future. My hope has always been that we could set up some form of organization, perhaps on a co-operative basis, in the two provinces where they must be able to sell potatoes if they are going to be able to stay on their farms, which would take control, and I think would pretty well relieve us here of the responsibility of considering this matter every year. I wanted to say that with regard to the general position.
Then, I have been asked questions as to why we have not consulted this one and why we have not consulted that one with regard to our activities in connection with certain matters.
Is it your opinion that, owing to the excellent quality of Simcoe county apples, you have never found it necessary to subsidize the farmers of Simcoe county?

That is not the major reason; but the fact is that during certain years we were subsidizing others we eliminated their apples from Ontario and Quebec, and left that market entirely to the Ontario and Quebec growers. Later on we did quota the number of apples which could be shipped from British Columbia or from the maritime provinces to Ontario and Quebec. And thus there has been left the best market in the world, right under their noses in Ontario and Quebec-Toronto, Montreal and elsewhere- to the people who produced the apples in Ontario. And I have sometimes wondered, in view of the fact that the apples up in
Supply-Agriculture
Simcoe are so good, why they buy so many British Columbia apples. But apparently that is a fact.
Just the spice of life; I suppose that is why. It is not the superior quality.

The question asked as to our consulting different people who are interested in the marketing of wheat as to the decisions made brings to my mind the fact that when we started to consider this question first we were confronted with a resolution which had been introduced into the legislature of Saskatchewan.
During our discussions reference has been made time and again to the possibility of this being somewhat of a political issue-that somebody's hide has got to be saved. Well, I think most of the members in the house, and particularly those from the west, will agree that I have never needed anybody to save my hide, politically. I have been running elections now for thirty-eight years, and I have won them all. So that there is not any hide-saving required. Last time I had the largest majority I ever had; so I am not worrying about that part of it.
Now, I do not know whether the legislature of Saskatchewan was playing politics with wheat or not. There was a suggestion made that there might be an election this summer. I have never agreed or never thought that there would be. As a matter of fact I have my own idea of when that election will be-and I do not think I will be more than a week out. But I am not going to announce it for the benefit of my hon. friends tonight.
The resolution which was introduced on February 21 into that legislature read like this:
What year?
We were talking about 1950.

And I am talking about 1951, which is more up to date. It said:
Mr. Thair, on Friday next, to move the following resolution:
That this assembly, recognizing that there exists a national responsibility to compensate the wheat producers for the heavy losses sustained under the Anglo-Canadian wheat agreement and in view of the fact that the farmers of Saskatchewan have carried an undue burden of consumer subsidization, recommend to the dominion government that a final payment of not less than 25 cents per bushel be made as a final payment under the five-year pool.
I would call attention to the fact that in this resolution they mention the heavy losses sustained under the Anglo-Canadian wheat agreement. That is the chief fact mentioned in the resolution. Then they go on to refer

Supply-Agriculture
to the question raised a few moments ago by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright), namely the subsidizing of the consumers in this country. Then they recommend a final payment of not less than 25 cents a bushel- which works out to about $350 million.
Well, it is true that that is not all suggested as a subsidy. There is 3 -81 cents of it already in the pool as a result of having sold wheat. So that, as was suggested the other night by the hon. member for Melfort, the subsidy is something over $300 million. That resolution was on the order paper of February 21. The Prime Minister stood up in this house on March 2 and made the announcement that we were paying $65 million into the pool which would result in a payment of about 8-3 cents per bushel on the wheat. On March 5, just three days later, this appears on the votes and proceedings of the legislature of Saskatchewan:
The motion, to be moved by Mr. Thair, respecting a final payment by the government of Canada, under the five-year wheat pool, of not less than 25 cents per bushel was, by leave of the assembly, withdrawn.
It remained on the order paper from February 21 until March 5, and then by leave of the house it was withdrawn. Then on March 6, the next day, Mr. Thair moved another resolution as follows:
Mr. Thair, on Thursday next, to move the following resolution:
That this assembly regrets that the government of Canada has failed to give the wheat growers a sufficient return for the wheat delivered to the five-year pool during the period 1945-49, and urges the said government to give immediate consideration to the revision upward of the 8-3 cents per bushel final payment recently announced, in order that the wheat growers may be more adequately compensated.
It will be seen that they have dropped all mention of the "have regard to" clause or of the British agreement. They did not want to talk about that. They even dropped all mention of the 25 cents per bushel and left our friends who sit in this house and who support the same party sitting holding the bag. There is no 25 cents mentioned in the resolution at all. Those men back in Regina who are close to the farming population of western Canada, who are close to the organizations that handle grain in great quantities, came to the conclusion that the 25 cents should not be there and they withdrew it from their resolution.
Apparently they did not know that I was going to make a speech in the house on Thursday, March 8, when they suggested putting this resolution on the order paper on Thursday, March 8. I made a speech on Thursday, March 8, which was published in Regina, and
[Mr Gardinei ]
instead of having the resolution proceeded with on Thursday, on March 9 this appears in the votes and proceedings:
By leave of the assembly, the resolution to be moved by Mr. Thair respecting the final settlement for wheat delivered to the five-year pool during the period 1945-49, was withdrawn.
It was withdrawn.
Was that a private member's motion?
You know Mr. Thair.
Was it a private member's motion?
It was a private member's motion, yes.
Private members withdraw their motions here.

But they do not do it that often and with the same relationship to what other people are saying. The speech which I delivered in the house that evening did lay some responsibility upon the British government for the decision reached. The resolution which was on the order paper or which my friend thought was on the order paper, but which from his attitude now and at the time he made his speech, he did not seem to know about-
As a matter of fact I did not know that those motions were on the paper.
I am beginning to think you did not, although I thought you had other ideas.
If the minister wants to start a debate on this I am sure we will be glad to accommodate him.
I am not starting anything, I am just trying to give information. I am giving it.
You have not given any explanation yet as to why the producers were not called in for consultation between May 22 and May 30, 1950.
I did not interrupt the hon. member when he was speaking.
This afternoon?
Not when you are giving so strong a speech as you were the other night and when you are far off the track as you were.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The minister was not here.
Some of our friends in the press gallery ought to realize you are not always on the track.
May I suggest that the minister address the chair.
Can't you take it?
I can quite understand why you do not like my looks. I will turn the other way.
Again I suggest that the minister should not address me personally but rather should speak to the chair. That is a rule of the house.
I looked right straight in your eyes the other night when you were saying that I was making statements that could not be believed.
That is right.

So that resolution was withdrawn on the day following the speech which I delivered in this house and in which I said that there was some responsibility on the British government. I refer now to votes and proceedings of the Regina house of Tuesday March 13, 1951. My friend made his speech in the house on the night of March 12 and it was reported in the Regina Leader-Post the next morning. There is no question about whether or not the members of the legislature of Saskatchewan, private or otherwise, knew of that speech and what was said. Let us read the third resolution they put on the order paper, after having withdrawn two. I am not too sure that this one is going to stick for reasons I happen to know about, but we will put it on the record anyway. The votes and proceedings of March 13 contains this:
Moved by Mr. Thair, seconded by Mr. Brown:
That this assembly endorses the resolution passed at a joint meeting of the Saskatchewan Federation of Agriculture and the executive of the western agricultural conference held in Regina on Wednesday, March 7, 1951, as follows:
"That the government of Canada be asked to pay on the five-year pool settlement at least 548,090,000 as a return of the subsidy paid by producers on domestic wheat, plus a further substantial payment in addition to the $65,000,000 token payment already announced in consideration of the 'have regard to' clause of the Canada-United Kingdom agreement".
If anybody can run an election on those resolutions I would like to see them try it. There is not going to be an election run on the wheat payment. There is not going to be any election run as a result of any vote that is passed here, whether it is $65 million or any other number of millions. The people who have been trying to build up that theory in the minds of the people are doing it without any knowledge of the facts, without having given any thought whatsoever to what is going on in the section of the country from which we come.
If in spite of what I am saying there happens to be an election in western Canada or in Saskatchewan two years before the time the government needs to have it, it certainly
Supply-Agriculture
will not be run on this issue. As someone said the other night, the issue upon which they are threatening to run is the Korean issue. When we see the Korean issue discussed in this house in order to obstruct the discussion of this particular resolution-

I rise to a question of privilege. The hon. member for Vancouver East certainly had no thought in mind of obstructing this discussion. As a matter of fact he did that on his own initiative. When the minister says that there is disagreement, look at the disagreement there is in the Liberal party tonight on this wheat issue.

Mr. Chairman, I probably have no right to suggest that the hon. member had any motive in mind when he discussed Korea this afternoon and I probably should withdraw the suggestion because it is not in accordance with the rules of the house. Nevertheless I would point out that the premier of Saskatchewan did suggest having an election on that issue.
No, that is not what he said.
From the floor of the house.
No, no.
On the issue of the activities in Korea.
That is not what he said.

This is sufficient for the purpose we have at the moment. The party that my hon. friend leads is not very well decided as to just what they think about wheat. I have been asked why we did not consult the farmers. Three members of this government did consult the farmers last week.
Ah, but-

We will get around to your "ah, but" after a while, but right now I am telling you that we did discuss it with the farmers. It may surprise my hon. friends when they go home at Easter to find out that what I stated here very early in the debate is true, namely, that I have not yet met a single farmer who was asking for 25 cents a bushel, and that I was much nearer right than some of the others are. That is the position in relation to this matter but I did not rise so much to deal with that. Many things have been said in this house with respect to myself personally and with regard to my general attitude toward this question. In that regard I want to say that a great deal has been said about the relationships of this country with Great Britain, and about the attitude that one should take towards discussions between this country and Great Britain.

Supply-Agriculture
I do not think I need to make any apologies to anyone-and more particularly to the leader of the C.C.F. party-for any attitude that I have ever taken towards Great Britain either in this house or outside of it. As a matter of fact I have perhaps a peculiar opinion in the minds of some people but I still believe in the good old theory that was enunciated many years ago by the leader of the Conservative party at that time when he said: "A British subject I was born and a British subject I hope to die."
I will die.
No, I read it myself today and he said "I hope to die."

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Speak for yourself.
Revised version.
There are more than modern members of parliament who get their Hansard, corrected at times.

You go and
look at the monument at Kingston. You will see which is right.

That was after it was revised, I suppose, but the way it is in Hansard is just as I have stated. What I wanted to say was that as a Canadian citizen I am also a British subject, and I think I am so recognized and acknowledged when I am in Great Britain. The British do not expect that we are going to take exactly the same attitude or feel ourselves under some obligation to withhold discussions in certain directions when we are in London as we might feel if we were in Moscow. There is a little different attitude taken by people in the capitals of the countries of the British commonwealth compared with people who are in other capitals. International complications are not the same.
That brings to my mind that when I turned on the radio on Sunday night to listen to the review of the news I heard the most scurrilous description of myself that I have ever heard, and I have heard a lot of them. This one was made by the son of one of the most gentlemanly individuals whom I have ever had the opportunity to meet in my political life, the former leader of the C.C.F. party. I do not know that I would have listened to it if I had known what he was going to say but once I started to listen I had to listen to the end to see how far he would go.
The editor of a Liberal paper.
That paper is not Liberal.
Since when?

The story was to the effect that there was something wrong with my morals. Well, probably there is but they will compare favourably with those of some other people. Then he went on to say that I was doing something which would injure international relationships. I want to tell the hon. gentleman-I don't know that I should give him that title because he does not sit in this house, and for that reason and no other probably-that after this speech which I have in my hand was delivered-
Which one is that?

I am going to read it to you and you will know all about it-I had to sit at a dinner in this city to which I was invited and listen to this man and his speech being criticized by the representatives of another nation. I had to apologize for him by saying that his opinion does not count for much anyway. Maybe on that basis I should not say anything about it in this house but nevertheless I have spoken to so many people who have stated in the last few days that I should say something about it that I want to read what this American gentleman was objecting to. This speech was delivered on December 17, 1950.
By whom?

By the editor of the Evening Citizen. Here is what he said, as reported in the Ottawa Citizen of December 19, 1950:
I do not think Canadians are more afraid than other people are of getting involved in another big war. What they are afraid of, I think, is that they may be dragged into a war that might be avoided if it were not for America's hysterical fear of communism and blunders in American foreign policy this fear has caused.
If I ever say anything in this house that is as strong as that, or anything that is more likely than that to cause trouble between two countries, then I will expect someone to make on the radio and elsewhere the kind of attack which was made by the editor of this paper in the city of Ottawa.

What has
that got to do with item 576?
My friend says: What has this got to do with this item? It was this very matter that he was discussing when he made this statement with regard to myself.
On December 19?

He said because I had suggested that $65 million was to be paid that it was immoral because it was being done to bribe people for this election that was going to be held. There were other reasons why it was immoral. It was a terrible thing to be doing at this time of difficulty throughout the world because of the effect it might have

internationally. I am just suggesting that if I had ever gone as far as this gentleman has gone in that direction I would not be surprised at anything that might be said.
Excommunicate him.

I have in my hand another publication which has been dealing with this question for some time. I think I should deal with it because it has been quoted twice tonight in the debate so far. There are some rather complimentary remarks made at the beginning of it by Mr. Michael Barkway in commenting upon the discussion in this house last week.
What I should like to say at the beginning is that in the 38 years that I have sat either in the legislature or in the House of Commons, on two occasions I have seen men brought before the bar of the house for disrespect to members who have been speaking in different legislative bodies. I doubt very much if they had gone any farther than, or as far as, either of these gentlemen did go with regard to discussions in this house recently. I am not going so far as to make statements in this house with regard to either of them that I would not make outside the house because I do not think it is fair for any member who is under the protection of the house to attack men who have not the protection of the house; but I do think it is most unfair for men, who are given the privilege of sitting in the press gallery of this house, to abuse that privilege by uttering statements which are not borne out by the facts in connection with any discussion which took place in this house. Therefore I think I must make the corrections that are necessary in order to make sure that these matters are not reported again in the discussion as being matters of fact. They are not matters of fact. This gentleman says:
There is nothing of finesse about Mr. Gardiner's technique.
He is not the only one who has said that.

I never pretend to be an after-dinner speaker or anything of that kind. I continue:
There is nothing of finesse about Mr. Gardiner's technique. "The British were confident," he said, "that the price of wheat would fall below $1.55 in the last two years of the agreement, and we were just as confident, that with United States aid and a Canadian loan, the price would go and remain above $1.55.''
Then there is a part put in which I am not sure that he could have said. It is in brackets to show something that is supposed to be in the agreement and I think it is. Then he goes on to say:
Probably no other member of parliament would have dared to bank on the shortness of public memory to this extent. In all parts of the house, 80709-95
Supply-Agriculture
members remembered perfectly well that in the years Mr. Gardiner was speaking of, 1945 and 1946, the one great fear of the farmers' organizations, and the one compelling motive for signing the four-year contract was the expectation that the bottom would drop out of the wheat market. Mr. Gardiner, who has an exceptionally good memory, must remember that in the summer of 1946 an international wheat agreement was already being discussed, and the price then being contemplated as a maximum was $1.55. He will also remember that the preamble to the United Kingdom agreement-
Said so and so. Let us take a look for a moment at the prices during the period of which he speaks and when he says the price was $1.55. The world price as we have been discussing it, the Chicago price, in September of 1945 was $1.72 when we started to discuss $1.55 as a ceiling. The price in June of 1946 was $1.95; at Chicago in July, 1946, it was $2.01. It was in July, 1946, that the contract was signed at $1.55. How anyone can suggest that there was any reason for considering $1.55 as the actual price of wheat, or anything associated with it, is most difficult to understand.
The next paragraph says that a world agreement was being discussed at that time, an international wheat agreement. An international wheat agreement was first discussed in 1932, and in case somebody looks up the record I had better recite it now. I was opposed to it and, as a matter of fact, led the attack upon it in the legislature of Saskatchewan when I was leading the opposition. That opposition to the agreement continued for some years, as members of the C.C.F. party know. But in recent years I have been a convert to the idea and you know converts always believe in anything much more firmly than those who had always believed in it.
And how!

And so I am somewhat of a convert. But what was the ceiling price that was being discussed? It was not $1.55 a bushel. It never was. The ceiling price being discussed at the beginning at that time was $1.50 a bushel, and the floor was $1 a bushel. And we in Canada agreed to accept that ceiling of $1.50 and the floor of $1. But when the matter went before the conference which was held, as he stated here, it was not agreed to. The reason that it was not agreed to was that the American parity price was $1.80; and they insisted upon the ceiling price in the agreement being $1.80; and not $1.55. I should like my friend to explain why, under these facts, he tries to tell me that we were absolutely convinced that at

Supply-Agriculture
that time wheat was only going to be worth $1.55. Then we come down to the next statement where he says:
As late as April, 1947, Mr. Gardiner said to the House of Commons: "If the world market remains as high as it is now, which very few people expect . .
He just cuts the sentence off there. I do not know what I said after that; I have not looked it up; but he says that in April 1947 I said: "If the world market remains as high as it is now, which very few people expect"- he says that in order to prove to the Canadian public that I had not thought wheat was going to stay up as compared with what it was at the beginning of this contract. Well, what was the price of wheat on the Chicago market in April of 1947? It was $2.58, and it continued to go up until it was $3.09 later in that year. Wheat never has been as high as that since. In other words, I said that wheat could not remain at the very high peak that it was in 1947. It was bound to come down from there, and it was because it was bound to come down from there that there was no reason in the world for being absolutely -convinced when we accepted $2 a bushel later on that that would not result in any payment being made under the "have regard to" clause. All I repeat this for is to indicate that that was the position.
In his next statement he goes on to say:
No wonder members found the rest of the argument topsy-turvy. But if Mr. Gardiner is anything, he is ingenious. By carefully chosen references he built up his precarious structure.
Someone quoted the remainder of this this evening indicating that I had left out something. The only thing I left out was what everybody agrees with regard to, namely, that a legal floor was established under the agreement and that the "have regard to" clause had relation to the ceiling and not to the floor, and therefore there was no reason whatsoever for my using this quotation in connection with what I had to say on the matter. But I would point this out, that the Canadian government put a floor under wheat before the British government put in any floor. We -put a floor of $1 per bushel for five years in 1945, to be continued until the end of the five-year pool. That floor which was there in the last year was an obligation to this government which the British government only accepted when they were drawing up this agreement, and the fact that they put $1.25 in the other was not going to be of any particular help to the farmers because we had already guaranteed them $1.25 for the whole five years of the contract.
Every member of this house recalls that we here passed an amendment to the act a year later than this contract was drawn

raising the advance payment from $1.25, where it had been and which was as high as the British ever put it, to $1.35. They had that guarantee right through the whole contract no matter what the British had undertaken to -put in it. I believe that is sufficient to cover that particular matter, but there is one other thing which is his final crack. He says this:
The other essential basis of Mr. Gardiner's argument was that the British government, in his own words, "owed us something or owed the farmers of western Canada something." But here he was up against the fact that last June 5, Mr. Howe, the minister responsible for marketing wheat, had told parliament that the British said they had fulfilled all their obligations; and Mr. Howe added: "We agreed on behalf of Canada that considering all the circumstances that was the case."
Now, here is the important thing.
Mr. Gardiner simply ignored this.
I have in my hand the Hansard, Mr. Chairman. What are the facts? I was being interrupted while I was attempting to put the whole matter on the record. I read the first two sentences, and then someone said something and I went on to read the other, "We agreed on behalf of Canada that considering all the circumstances that was the case." This man says I passed that up altogether. He says I passed it up as part of my technique. I am not going to say anything more with regard to the remainder of the article, because it deals with Mr. Howe's position, other than to say this to the members of this committee, that the Minister of Trade and Commerce on two occasions corrected that statement. The statement was repeated here a few minutes ago by the member for Melfort. On two occasions the Minister of Trade and Commerce corrected that statement before someone said to him, "Well, do you want to correct it?" Mr. Howe said no. He had already corrected it. He corrected it again later on.
All I want to say about it is, that under those circumstances I think an article of this kind is so far away from the facts that the gentleman who wrote it ought to get the information and read it himself. This afternoon someone said that the information is all on the record. There is information on the record with regard to one incident, and after that information was placed in the hands of the committee the mover of the resolution requesting the information withdrew the resolution and the other information is not in the hands of the committee. But that information only bears out what has been said; and, Mr. Chairman, I am not going to go any further into the discussion than to say that there are no two members of this government-I want to say this-there are no two members of this government who

have worked more closely over the last fifteen years than the Minister of Trade and Commerce and myself. I do want to say this, too, that I have never made a move in connection with this wheat matter without first discussing it with the Minister of Trade and Commerce, since he became the Minister of Trade and Commerce. We discussed all these matters as I indicated in the story I told more than a week ago, and which has been the subject of criticism in this house. As was demonstrated this afternoon, the members who got up and made criticisms had not read Hansard themselves. I would suggest that if criticisms are going to be made, that really ought to be done. I make no apology whatever for taking up a little time tonight in order to straighten out one or two things. I have never asked for anyone's sympathy-
Indulgence.

-indulgence, yes, that is probably the better word-at any time since I have been in this house or at any time since I have been in politics. I have always attempted to keep myself informed before I tried to inform others. I should like to suggest to those who are going to write articles like this that they ought to have themselves informed before they write them.
For the benefit of my hon. friend, I am going to tell a little story. There is another periodical that is printed not very far away from where this one is printed. On two occasions that periodical undertook to write articles like this one. One occasion was when I was fighting a battle in Saskatchewan in 1929, and I am not going over the details of it now, but the most scurrilous attack prior to this one and prior to the one on Sunday night that has ever been made upon me-I think they have been just as scurrilous upon me as anyone else-was made on that occasion. We lost the election. Then, we had another election five years later, and we won that. The same gentleman wrote the same kind of article again. He could not understand why the Saskatchewan people would put me back again.
Do you know what happened? That periodical was thrown off most of the newsstands in Saskatchewan; they said they would not sell it.
What was the name of that periodical?
It was Maclean's magazine.
It still survived, you know.
Which newspapers?
One of them was a Liberal paper and the other was a Conservative paper.
What are the names?

The first was the Leader-Post of its day and the second was the Regina Star of its day. There is not anyone in the newspaper business who will question the fact that both of the machines that were set up around them were smashed. My difficulty is that some of those associated with these ventures are still alive and scattered over Canada, and some of them are still in the newspaper business.
You would rather that they were dead, I suppose.

I do not worry about them. They elect me every election. I just wanted to state these facts in order to indicate to the members of this chamber that I am not

Supply-Agriculture
at all concerned about what these men write, but I am concerned about the welfare of the House of Commons which carries on discussions regarding public affairs and then has reports put out from these galleries by persons who pay no attention whatever to the facts when they have some reason for trying to propagandize someone out of this house or someone out of this government. But again I say that we in this country are in the fortunate position that we have a Liberal party and it believes in Liberal principles. This afternoon I said something which I probably did not make complete, and I want to complete it now. The Prime Minister, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, I and every other member of this government believe in the principles of Liberalism.
Why do you not live up to them?

We are out and out Liberals; and the essence of Liberalism is that you are out for reform. When you are out for reform, you are always pulling into the future. You are not always in agreement on what is being done today, although you hope to be all in agreement when what is advocated is accomplished and on what is being done after it is accomplished. We have all been working together in the government toward a certain end. If I were looking for compliments, and wanting to acknowledge them, I would say that the finest compliment that I have ever had since I have been in public life-and as I said a moment ago, I have been in public life now for 38 years-was the speech of the Minister of Trade and Commerce the other night in this chamber when he got to his feet and said what he did. He said what? He said that, even although he did not advocate it when we started, there had been a five-year pool set up, a year later there was a British contract drawn, and that this contract and this pool had been the best things that had ever been done in the interest of the wheat growers of western Canada. It just so happens that I was entrusted with the task of establishing the wheat pool; that is the five-year pool. It just so happens also that I was entrusted with the task of establishing the four-year contract; and that is the reason why I am entrusted with the task tonight of trying to put through the $65 million vote which is the final act in connection with that contract.
You did a good job.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce says I did a good job.
Would you read us the last sentence of his speech?
The last sentence of his speech will stand a lot of investigation on the part of a man like the hon. member; and if he fully understands it-

Will the
minister read it?

I will read some other parts of the speech in which the Minister of Trade and Commerce said that, in spite of the fact that he felt this and he felt that, he was in agreement with the fact that the government had decided to pay $65 million into this pool.
Yes; he said that.
And that is all that is involved now.

Will the
minister read the last sentence?
If you read the whole speech you will be better informed than you will be by just reading the last sentence.
Read the last sentence.

As I say, that is the present position; and so far as the party itself is concerned I think that the party, led as it is, is one of the strongest parties we have ever had in Canada under any name. I also think that it would be weakened if any one of the three men who are being discussed so much in connection with this debate were to drop out of the party. I want to assure my hon. friends, however, that if I were out of the government tomorrow I would not drop out of the party. I would be hammering the Tories and the C.C.F.'ers just as strongly as when I was in the government. As long as the three of us remain where we are, I think it will be fairly generally agreed across the country that we have an exceedingly good government.

Really, Mr. Chairman, I never know just how to describe the minister, whether as irrepressible or incorrigible. I think one of those two words suits him tonight. What I really rose to say was this. I am wondering if the minister is trying to talk out his own resolution.
We can still put it through if you sit down.

The hon. member for Melfort asked the minister two questions, and I have repeated them. I would ask him to answer those two questions when we meet tomorrow afternoon. One is why no advice was sought from representatives of the producers between May 22 and May 30 before the government's acceptance of the final settlement; and second, why the amount which is owing to western

farmers for their contribution to Canadian bread during the years that were mentioned of approximately $48 million has not been included in that estimate. May I tell the minister that I read Hansard and that when I heard the sentence he extracted from Mr. Howe's statement this afternoon, I did not recognize it because it was taken out of its context; when read in the context, it means something different from what the minister said it meant and supports my view and not his.
Item stands.
Resolutions adopted in committee of supply this day reported, read the second time and concurred in.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
the adjournment of the house.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I generally announce a great many measures for the next day; but tonight I think I should limit myself to mentioning continuation of consideration of these supplementary estimates.
Some time ago the motion was passed that the house would adjourn tomorrow at six o'clock. I would suggest that if we got through with the estimates about six o'clock, we might get unanimous consent to sit a little longer so that these bills may be sent to the Senate.
Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Does the hon. member say he would not wish to have the supple-mentaries passed?
Tonight. This afternoon most of us were co-operating to get these estimates through. Tonight we have heard an hour-long speech from the Minister of Agriculture.
An hour and a quarter.
And I do not propose to sit tomorrow night under those circumstances.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I add a word. In connection with these supplementary estimates, I think we will have to sit Thursday or whatever time is necessary, until the supplementary estimates are passed. I am going to be here all the time, through Easter. I am not leaving. I hope the house will work to pass the balance of the estimates as soon as possible.
We listened to an hour-and-a-quarter long political speech.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Hon. members can talk as long as they like, but I point out that the supplementary- estimates must be passed before we adjourn for Easter.
Business of the House

May I point out that if there is any problem arising, then it is the entire responsibility of the government. The Minister of Agriculture has talked for an hour and a quarter about everything except wheat.
I talked an hour about wheat.
He conducted a filibuster against his own estimates; and if there is any responsibility it must rest entirely upon the Minister of Agriculture.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I suggest that I understand that after a speech like that of the Minister of Agriculture some people are a little nervous. Tomorrow-
No, not nervous at all; but it did not relate to wheat.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I would not want to have a quick decision made, and I would not think this would be the proper time to make it. But I suggest that from now until tomorrow at three o'clock we think this over; because the passing of the supplementary estimates for this year is a quite important matter, and the consequences ought to be thought about. As to responsibility, we will not go into any long speeches. I have listened to a good many of them.
One tonight.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, and from the hon. member for Eglinton nearly every day.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The house is
adjourned until tomorrow at three o'clock.

Before the house adjourns, it is all very well to make light of it. But the Minister of Agriculture to his own satisfaction has conducted a campaign this evening against the government of Saskatchewan, and against several responsible newspapers, and has discussed everything but wheat. If there is going to be any problem arising, then the Minister of Agriculture might well consider the course that he himself has perhaps made necessary, and that is letting this item stand by itself, in relation to the other items before us.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If we could agree, we could continue sitting tonight.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We could sit for an hour tonight.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Easter does not begin until Friday.

We listened to an hour-and-a-quarter political speech tonight, and I am not going to agree to that sort of thing. If

Business of the House we get that kind of treatment, we have some rights in this house and we are going to insist upon having them respected.
Mr. Speaker-
Eleven o'clock.
I think my hon. friend will agree-
You made a good speech.

-that I took quite a bit last week; and I do not know why they should not be prepared to listen to my answer, especially when I took it from those outside the house who could not be answered any other place but here. I think I had the right to say what I had to say tonight; and I would just like to suggest that I think what the minister his just said is perhaps true. We may feel better tomorrow; and if I took up too much time tonight, then could we meet at eleven o'clock tomorrow, or some other time to discuss the matter.
But the minister's speech deliberately played Saskatchewan politics.
No.
It did.
And I have nothing to do with the legislature of Saskatchewan.
Eleven o'clock.

I have nothing whatever to do with it. I did not know those private members' motions were on the order paper, incidentally. And to drag such a matter extraneously into the house, and then expect us to accommodate the minister and the government by sitting tomorrow night is, I think, something that we should not tolerate.
To accommodate the people of Canada.

I would say to my hon. friend that I did not refer to the scurrilous attack he made upon me the other night. I think he will agree that probably I had sufficient reason to have done so; but I did not.
I am very anxious to see this $65 million item pass but my previous criticisms are justified by the record.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Let us finish it then.
But I think there is a point beyond which we should not retreat in circumstances such as these.
Retreat?

It being five minutes after eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
